title: Chapter 9. When people do not leave home: they travel in the virtual

blocks.text: “When people do not leave home: they travel in the virtual.” Pedro's sentence describes a gesture that is no longer a novelist's: putting on a headset, or opening a window on the screen, and being, in some way, somewhere else. Walking through a museum in another city, or another century. Walking down a street that is not yours. Sitting, in a digital world, with people who do not have to take a train in order to meet. Seeing the Earth, even the Moon of the previous chapter, without leaving the chair. Travel no longer necessarily asks for a ticket, a saved-up wage, a suitcase and the permission of a work calendar. For a book that has criticised the four coins, that possibility is not a small one: if moving through the world ceases to cost a fortune in time and money, part of the blackmail loosens.

blocks.text: Here too a nuance is needed. Staying at home can be a freedom and can be a confinement. The same headset that opens a museum can close the street door. This chapter wants both halves: the advantages, which are real, and the risk of isolation, which is real as well.

blocks.text: What already exists need not be dreamed. For years large and small museums have been digitising rooms, pictures, objects, and offering visits on the web. The Prado, the Louvre, so many others, can be walked through, at least in part, from a room. During the COVID-19 pandemic that gesture ceased to be a luxury and became, for millions of people, the only way not to lose culture altogether. UNESCO, in a report of May 2020, estimated that nearly 90 per cent of the world's museums — more than 85,000 institutions — closed their doors during the crisis, and that the sector reacted quickly by developing its presence on the Internet. The same report, and the notes that accompanied it, warned of a gap: only 5 per cent of museums in Africa and in small island developing states were able to offer content online. In 2021, a second UNESCO report put the average closure of museums in 2020 at 155 days, and the average drop in attendance at the beginning of 2021, when many closed again, at 70 per cent. The lesson is double. The virtual can hold a thread when the building shuts. And that thread does not reach everyone equally: without a connection, without a device, without skills, the digital journey does not exist. Almost half of humanity, UNESCO recalled then, had no access to the Internet. A book that speaks of travelling without leaving home cannot forget those who have no digital house.

blocks.text: Virtual reality, in the narrower sense — that of headsets that occupy the field of view, the audio, sometimes the hands — has left the laboratory and the video game. It is used to train, to operate at a distance, to teach anatomy, so that an older person may walk along a beach they can no longer set foot on. There are studies, still modest in size and in reach, that point to benefits. A 2023 review of the use of virtual reality in care homes for older people, published in a geriatric research setting, concluded, from 22 articles, that VR was a promising intervention to reduce isolation and loneliness and improve social engagement, though it also found barriers: adaptation to the technology, the quality of the image, the culture of the institution. A 2023 paper in Scientific Reports, with 74 people who socialised on the Altspace VR platform during the pandemic, found lower levels of loneliness and social anxiety inside the virtual world than outside it, especially among those who met a regular group; the research itself warned of the limits of the sample and of generalisation. These are not universal proofs. They are signs that, for some people and in some circumstances, the virtual does not replace a hug and, even so, eases.

blocks.text: One can, then, visit a museum, learn a craft, see a landscape, try out a journey, meet strangers who cease to be strangers, without paying for a plane and without asking for a day off. For whoever cannot travel, that is not a frivolity. It is a door. For whoever wants to meet someone who lives a thousand kilometres away, it is a square. For whoever wishes to see the room of a museum they do not have next door, it is a piece of luck. Pedro includes in that possibility that of not leaving home and, even so, not being left without a world. In an essay that has spoken of abundance, of AI and of time recovered, virtual travel is a way of spending that time on something other than the shopping of the small hours.

blocks.text: The risk, now, without frightening and without denying. A window is not a path. If the window becomes the only landscape, the house closes. The body, which this book has defended against the rental of the wage, also asks for the street, the shore, the air, the brush of others in a space that cannot be switched off with a button. Problematic use of the Internet, which we already saw in chapter 5 — 3.7 per cent of adults aged 15 to 64 in EDADES 2024, and 11.7 per cent among the youngest — recalls that the web can trap. Virtual reality, being more enveloping, can trap more, or can, paradoxically, give a relief that is then not translated into going out. Isolation is not always felt as isolation. Sometimes it is felt as comfort. One stops going to the square because the square fits in the living room, and one day discovers that the habit of the real square has been lost, the one that smells, that inconveniences, that surprises.

blocks.text: There is another trap, closer to the critique of money. Digital worlds can also be priced, rented, filled with shop windows. One can travel in the virtual and, even so, be shopping. One can meet people and, even so, be alone, if the meeting is designed to retain, not to find. The same warning of chapter 5 holds here: that the tool not become the master. That the headset come off. That the lagoon, which is not virtual, still have someone who treads it and someone who cares for it.

blocks.text: Pedro's proposal, read with that nuance, is not that people should never go out. It is that they should be able not to go out when they cannot, or when they do not want to spend their life on journeys, and that, even so, they should travel, learn, gather. “They do not leave home” is a possibility, not a banishment. The house, if it is good, is a centre, not a cage. From a house beside the Mar Menor one can walk through a museum on another shore and, on taking off the headset, go out and see the real water, which has no resolution or latency, only swell. That coming and going — from the virtual to the real, and back again — would be the health of the invention. The danger would be to choose only one side.

blocks.text: Travelling in the virtual can be a form of justice: the journey of whoever does not have the four coins for the other journey, or does not have the body for the platform, or does not have a visa, or does not have time because the wage has eaten it. It can be a form of knowledge and of friendship. It can, badly used, be one more way of not being present. This book, as it closes this chapter, keeps all three sentences at once, because all three are true. And it leaves the shore where it was: a step from home, in case one feels like going out.

blocks.text: A closing image remains, which brings the journey back to this district. A virtual museum of Cartagena or of Tyre, a reconstructed Phoenician street, a square where one speaks with someone who lives on the other side of the Mediterranean, and then, on taking off the headset, the real walk to the shore. The virtual would have widened the day. The real would have confirmed it. If that to-and-fro becomes a custom, people will not have stopped leaving home: they will have left in more than one way. If the second movement is lost, that of the door and of the salt, then we shall indeed have travelled so much that we are no longer anywhere. This book, which began with a face-to-face deal, prefers that the journey, even if it is digital, should not erase our face.

blocks.text: Technology, in this, is not a fate. It is a means. It can be used to open the world to whoever cannot travel, and it can be used so that no one meets in the street any more. The difference will not be made by the headset. It will be made by the use, and it will be made by a society that still knows how to invite people out, not only to log on.
